title: Diabetic Ketoacidosis - New Type 1 Diabetes (Rural Explanation and Management)
patient_instructions: You are Karen Mitchell, the mother of Emily, a 17-year-old girl who has just been brought into the small rural hospital where you farm, about four hours (400 km) from the nearest big-city hospital. Over the last two weeks Emily has been drinking huge amounts of water, going to the toilet constantly, and has lost weight. Today she collapsed out on the farm and you rushed her in. The doctors have told you her blood sugar is very high. You are frightened and overwhelmed. You want to understand: What is wrong with her? What do the blood tests mean? What are they going to do right now? Is she going to be alright, and will she have this forever? You have no medical background, so you need plain-language explanations. If the candidate uses jargon (ketones, acidosis, VBG), ask them what it means. There is no family history of diabetes. Emily has otherwise been well, no recent obvious infection that you noticed. Affect: anxious, tearful at times, but reassured by a calm, clear doctor who sits down and lets you tell the story first.
candidate_instructions: You are the doctor in a rural emergency department, approximately 400 km (4 hours) from the nearest tertiary centre. Emily Mitchell, 17, has been diagnosed with diabetic ketoacidosis as the first presentation of type 1 diabetes (BGL 35 mmol/L, blood ketones 4 mmol/L, venous pH 7.15, potassium 6 mmol/L). She is being resuscitated. Her mother, Karen, is at the bedside and very anxious. Your tasks: (1) Explain the investigations and the diagnosis to the mother. (2) Explain the immediate management. (3) Outline the long-term management of type 1 diabetes and address the rural transfer plan. You have 8 minutes.
examiner_instructions: This station tests clear lay explanation of DKA and its emergency and long-term management in a rural setting. Reward the candidate for: sitting down, building rapport and inviting the mother to summarise events; explaining in plain language that blood sugar is very high, the body burns fat producing ketones, ketones make the blood acidic (low pH on VBG), and salts are being watched. The diagnosis should be stated as DKA confirming type 1 diabetes using the paediatric/RCH triad - hyperglycaemia (BGL >11 mmol/L), acidosis (venous pH <7.3 or bicarbonate <15 mmol/L), and ketosis (ketones >=3 mmol/L). Management: IV normal saline first with slow deficit correction over ~48 h and no boluses unless shocked; insulin infusion started only after the first hour and NEVER as a bolus; potassium withheld while K is 6 mmol/L and anuria excluded, added once K <5.5 mmol/L and urine output present; hourly monitoring; watch for cerebral oedema. Rural plan: stabilise locally, consult the paediatric team, transfer to tertiary care. Correct any statement that pH just under 7.4 is diagnostic (normal venous pH ~7.32-7.38; threshold is <7.3) or that bicarbonate <18 is the paediatric cut-off (use <15). Prompt if needed: 'What complication are you most worried about?'

criteria: Sits down, builds rapport, invites the parent to summarise events and acknowledges her distress
Explains investigations in plain language: very high blood sugar, ketones from fat breakdown, acidic blood on the VBG, salts monitored
Checks understanding throughout and avoids or defines jargon
Names diabetic ketoacidosis as the diagnosis and explains it confirms new type 1 diabetes (insulin deficiency)
States the paediatric diagnostic triad correctly: hyperglycaemia (BGL >11 mmol/L), acidosis (venous pH <7.3 or bicarbonate <15 mmol/L), ketosis (ketones >=3 mmol/L)
Interprets the VBG correctly (normal venous pH ~7.32-7.38; this pH 7.15 indicates acidosis) without over-calling
Identifies and plans to treat a precipitant (infection or, in established diabetes, insulin omission) with a septic screen
Fluids first: IV normal saline before insulin, correcting the deficit slowly over ~48 h with no boluses unless shocked
Insulin infusion started only after the first hour, titrated to lower glucose gradually, with glucose added as BGL falls; never an IV insulin bolus in paediatric DKA
Potassium managed correctly: withhold while K is 6 mmol/L / anuric, add KCl once K <5.5 mmol/L and passing urine; recognises total-body potassium depletion
Hourly monitoring of BGL, ketones, potassium, renal function, urine output and neurological status

Recognises cerebral oedema as the key life-threatening complication (first ~12 h) with early signs (headache, irritability, lethargy, vomiting) and escalates immediately with hyperosmolar therapy/airway support
Rural plan: stabilise locally, consult paediatric team, transfer to tertiary centre given limited hourly biochemical monitoring
Uses clear, empathic, jargon-free language appropriate to a frightened parent

Outlines long-term type 1 management: insulin (MDI or pump), multidisciplinary team (endocrinologist, diabetes educator, dietitian), sick-day plan, hypoglycaemia recognition and support (Diabetes Australia)

red_flags: Cerebral oedema - key life-threatening DKA complication, usually within the first 12 hours; early signs are headache, irritability, lethargy and vomiting after therapy starts
Hyperkalaemia/hypokalaemia - potassium of 6 mmol/L with total-body potassium depletion; first sign of a dangerous shift may be a fatal arrhythmia, so monitor hourly
Severe acidosis (venous pH <7.1) or haemodynamic compromise mandating tertiary transfer and intensive monitoring
Missed or untreated precipitant (infection or insulin omission) allowing DKA to progress
australian_guidelines: RCH / ISPAD paediatric DKA guideline - diagnostic triad: hyperglycaemia BGL >11 mmol/L, acidosis venous pH <7.3 or bicarbonate <15 mmol/L, ketosis blood ketones >=3 mmol/L; severity graded by pH (mild <7.3, moderate <7.2, severe <7.1)

RCH DKA management guideline - fluids before insulin, correct deficit slowly over ~48 h, insulin infusion after the first hour (never a bolus), withhold potassium until K <5.5 mmol/L and passing urine, hourly monitoring for cerebral oedema

RCH transfer criteria - consult the paediatric team for all children with DKA and all newly diagnosed diabetes; transfer for age <2 y, coma, cardiovascular compromise, seizures, cerebral oedema, or pH <7.1 / HCO3 <5

Therapeutic Guidelines (eTG) / Diabetes Australia - long-term type 1 care: insulin (MDI or pump), multidisciplinary diabetes team, structured education, sick-day plan and hypoglycaemia management with glucagon
learning_objectives: Explain DKA, its investigations and diagnosis to a distressed parent in plain language
Apply the correct paediatric DKA diagnostic thresholds (venous pH <7.3, bicarbonate <15 mmol/L, ketones >=3 mmol/L)
Sequence emergency DKA management safely: fluids first, delayed insulin infusion, careful potassium handling, and vigilance for cerebral oedema
Formulate a rural stabilise-and-transfer plan and outline long-term type 1 diabetes care
key_points: Fluids before insulin; start insulin only after the first hour and never as an IV bolus in paediatric DKA
Correct the deficit slowly (~48 h) and avoid boluses unless shocked to reduce the risk of cerebral oedema
Potassium may be high, normal or low but total-body potassium is always depleted; withhold while K >5.5 mmol/L or anuric, then replace
Cerebral oedema is the leading cause of DKA death in children - act on early neurological signs before imaging
Rural reality: limited hourly biochemistry means stabilise locally, consult paediatrics, and transfer to a tertiary centre

citations.claim: Diabetic ketoacidosis is a recognised complication of (particularly type 1) diabetes, consistent with the case's diagnosis and classification.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.1508

citations.claim: Potassium must be monitored intensively in DKA because hyperkalaemia is a medical emergency whose first sign may be a fatal arrhythmia/cardiac arrest - underpinning hourly potassium monitoring and withholding potassium when K is 6 mmol/L.
Acid-base interpretation relies on the venous/arterial pH (a low pH indicating acidosis) as read on the blood gas, supporting correct interpretation of the acidotic VBG in DKA.
